difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring identification of a self-selection confound: patients who seek out experimental treatments differ systematically from those who don't, so trial success doesn't translate to population-wide benefit.
stimulus: Patients with chronic migraines who voluntarily enroll in experimental acupuncture trials report a 40 percent reduction in headache frequency, a rate far exceeding that seen in standard pharmaceutical treatments. Yet when health insurers began covering acupuncture for all chronic migraine patients — not just volunteers — average headache frequency across the covered population decreased by less than 5 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acupuncture requires multiple sessions before any therapeutic effect is observed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only patients who already believe strongly in acupuncture's efficacy choose to enroll in experimental trials, and such belief itself contributes significantly to treatment success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Health insurers covering acupuncture reimburse practitioners at lower rates than trials do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic migraine is more prevalent among women than among men.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The acupuncture protocols used in experimental trials are more rigorous than those used in standard clinical settings.

explanations.correct: If trial enrollees are self-selected believers whose belief itself drives improvement, their superior outcomes reflect the selection effect rather than the treatment. Mandatory coverage extends acupuncture to skeptics who lack that belief-driven boost, collapsing the population-wide effect. Both facts are reconciled.
explanations.A: This applies equally to trial participants and to the broadly covered population, so it cannot explain why one group improves far more than the other.
explanations.C: Lower reimbursement might affect practitioner quality, but this addresses only the covered-population side without explaining the magnitude of the trial benefit — a 'resolves one horn only' trap.
explanations.D: Gender prevalence is irrelevant to the discrepancy between trial outcomes and population outcomes.
explanations.E: Protocol rigor could partly explain the difference, but it doesn't account for why trial volunteers see a 40% improvement that is independently linked to their being volunteers — it leaves the self-selection mechanism unnamed and thus resolves only one horn.

difficultyReason: Economic paradox involving reverse causation: the direction of causality between the observed variables is the opposite of what the surface reading implies.
stimulus: In the Ralston manufacturing sector, firms that pay wages in the top quartile for their industry experience employee turnover rates roughly half those of firms paying median wages. Yet when the Ralston government mandated an industry-wide wage floor that raised median pay to the former top-quartile level, overall employee turnover rates did not decline at all.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-wage firms in Ralston also tend to offer better retirement benefits than low-wage firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wage floor was difficult to enforce in small manufacturing firms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Firms that originally paid top-quartile wages did so because they also maintained distinctive cultures of employee recognition and career development that lower-wage firms never adopted when wages were equalized.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some Ralston manufacturing firms relocated operations to neighboring regions following the wage mandate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employee turnover in Ralston increased slightly in the year before the wage mandate was introduced.

explanations.correct: High-wage firms retained employees because of a bundle of advantages — recognition, career development, culture — that accompanied high wages but were not caused by them. When lower-wage firms were forced to match wages without adopting those other practices, the retention benefit did not transfer. Both facts are explained.
explanations.A: Better retirement benefits could be part of a confounding bundle, but this answer alone is too narrow to dissolve the paradox; it still leaves unexplained why equalizing wages didn't equalize retention.
explanations.B: Enforcement difficulty is irrelevant to the discrepancy unless we know firms actually circumvented the floor, which is not stated — a classic 'irrelevant' trap.
explanations.D: Relocation would reduce the number of firms but doesn't explain unchanged turnover rates among remaining firms — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.E: A pre-mandate trend worsens rather than resolves the paradox by suggesting conditions were already deteriorating before wages rose.

difficultyReason: Environmental science paradox requiring identification of a temporal scope difference: short-term and long-term ecological dynamics operate by different mechanisms.
stimulus: Forests that experience low-intensity prescribed burns every three years have significantly higher biodiversity than unburned forests in the same region. Yet ecologists monitoring the same burned forests report that immediately following each burn, the total number of animal species observed drops sharply for a period of six to eight months.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prescribed burns are conducted during seasons when most migratory species have already departed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drop in observed species immediately after a burn reflects temporary displacement rather than mortality, and the periodic clearing of underbrush allows habitat diversity to increase over the longer term, attracting more species than were present before burning began.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unburned forests accumulate leaf litter that eventually suppresses ground-cover plant growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prescribed burn programs are expensive to administer and require specialized forestry personnel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some animal species are attracted to forest areas immediately after a burn because of increased food availability.

explanations.correct: The answer bridges both time scales: the short-term drop is displacement (not extinction), and the long-term gain is structural habitat improvement. This reconciles the immediate post-burn decline with the superior overall biodiversity of burned forests.
explanations.A: Migratory departure explains a subset of the post-burn count decline, but doesn't address why burned forests ultimately have higher biodiversity than unburned ones — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.C: Leaf litter suppression helps explain why unburned forests are less biodiverse, but says nothing about the immediate post-burn species drop — still 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.D: Administrative cost is entirely irrelevant to the ecological paradox.
explanations.E: This actually deepens the paradox by suggesting species numbers should rise, not fall, immediately after a burn.

difficultyReason: Legal/policy paradox involving a definitional mismatch: what 'compliance' means in the statute versus what prosecutors measure differs in a way that explains the divergent outcomes.
stimulus: A study of contract disputes in Verano found that firms using standardized legal templates drafted by certified attorneys lose arbitration proceedings at a rate 30 percent lower than firms drafting their own contracts. Nonetheless, after Verano enacted a law requiring all commercial contracts to use certified templates, the overall rate at which firms lost arbitration proceedings was unchanged.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arbitration panels in Verano are composed of retired judges who are familiar with standardized template language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before the law, only firms with sophisticated legal departments chose to use certified templates, and those firms also prepared stronger documentary evidence and negotiated more favorable contract terms independently of the templates themselves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Certified legal templates are updated annually to reflect changes in Verano commercial law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cost of hiring certified attorneys to draft templates increased after the mandate took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arbitration proceedings in Verano increased in number following the enactment of the template requirement.

explanations.correct: Firms that voluntarily used templates were already legally sophisticated; the templates correlated with, but did not cause, arbitration success. When all firms were required to use templates, legally unsophisticated firms gained the template but not the surrounding expertise, so the population-wide loss rate stayed flat. Both facts are reconciled.
explanations.A: Panel familiarity with template language would predict improvement after the mandate, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.C: Annual updates are irrelevant to the discrepancy between voluntary-use outcomes and mandatory-use outcomes.
explanations.D: Increased cost might deter compliance but doesn't explain why mandatory templates failed to improve outcomes for compliant firms — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.E: A volume increase in proceedings is irrelevant to the rate at which firms lost those proceedings.

difficultyReason: Technology paradox requiring a measurement artifact explanation: what is being counted differs between the two contexts in a non-obvious way.
stimulus: Software engineers who use AI-assisted coding tools complete individual programming tasks roughly 55 percent faster than engineers who do not use such tools. Yet companies that have fully deployed AI coding assistants across their engineering teams report no significant reduction in the time required to ship completed software products.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AI-assisted code requires more extensive peer review and quality-assurance testing because it produces a higher volume of code — including bugs — per unit time, consuming the hours saved in individual task completion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: AI coding tools are more effective for routine tasks than for novel algorithmic problems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies that adopt AI tools tend to be larger and therefore have more complex coordination requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Engineers who use AI tools report higher job satisfaction than those who do not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cost of AI coding tool licenses is partially offset by reductions in engineer overtime hours.

explanations.correct: If AI tools accelerate code production but simultaneously generate more defects requiring review and testing, the downstream QA bottleneck absorbs the upstream time savings. Individual task speed rises while total product delivery time stays constant — both facts are reconciled by this measurement-scope mechanism.
explanations.B: Task-type limitations explain why gains might be modest, but do not explain why overall delivery time shows zero reduction at all — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.C: Company size is a confounding variable for coordination, but this introduces an entirely separate factor rather than explaining how faster individual tasks fail to produce faster shipping — an 'irrelevant' trap.
explanations.D: Job satisfaction is entirely unrelated to the delivery-time discrepancy.
explanations.E: Cost offsets and overtime say nothing about delivery timelines — irrelevant to the stated paradox.

difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox requiring a contextual difference explanation: the populations compared differ in a hidden dimension that explains divergent outcomes.
stimulus: Children raised in bilingual households acquire their first language's vocabulary more slowly on average than children raised in monolingual households, as measured at age three. Yet by age seven, bilingual children perform as well as or better than monolingual peers on standardized tests of first-language vocabulary.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Standardized vocabulary tests administered at age seven are calibrated to monolingual norms and may undercount bilingual children's total lexical knowledge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In bilingual households, children allocate cognitive resources across two languages simultaneously, slowing early first-language acquisition; however, the cross-linguistic structural knowledge built during this period accelerates vocabulary acquisition in both languages during the school years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bilingual children are more likely than monolingual children to attend multilingual school programs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: First-language vocabulary size at age three is not a reliable predictor of academic performance in secondary school.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parents in bilingual households read aloud to their children less frequently than parents in monolingual households.

explanations.correct: The answer explains the age-three lag (split cognitive resources across two languages) and the age-seven catch-up (cross-linguistic knowledge accelerates later acquisition), bridging both halves of the paradox through a single developmental mechanism.
explanations.A: If tests undercount bilingual knowledge, that would predict bilingual children actually score lower even at seven — this resolves one horn but potentially deepens the other by questioning whether the age-seven parity is real.
explanations.C: Multilingual school programs might accelerate catch-up but don't explain the early lag, leaving the first horn unaddressed — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.D: Academic performance in secondary school is outside the scope of the vocabulary paradox entirely — irrelevant.
explanations.E: Less frequent read-alouds would predict persistent deficits, deepening the paradox rather than resolving it.

difficultyReason: History/policy paradox requiring a reverse-causation or hidden-third-factor explanation: the relationship between two historical variables runs contrary to intuition.
stimulus: Historical records show that in the Aldenmoor region during the 1800s, towns with the highest rates of church attendance also had the highest rates of property crime. Yet sociologists universally agree that shared moral frameworks reduce antisocial behavior.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Churches in the Aldenmoor region during this period preached sermons that explicitly condemned property crime.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The towns with the highest church attendance in Aldenmoor were also the most densely populated and economically impoverished, conditions independently associated with elevated property crime rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Property crime records from the 1800s are less accurate than modern crime statistics because reporting rates were lower.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some Aldenmoor residents attended church specifically to establish trustworthy reputations that they then exploited for financial gain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Church attendance in Aldenmoor declined significantly during periods of economic prosperity.

explanations.correct: A hidden confounding variable — urban density and poverty — independently drives both high church attendance (community institution in struggling areas) and high property crime. Once that common cause is identified, the correlation between church attendance and crime no longer conflicts with the sociological principle, because church attendance is not reducing crime relative to what it would be without churches in those conditions.
explanations.A: Churches condemning crime is consistent with the sociological principle but deepens the paradox by making it even harder to explain why high-attendance towns still had more crime.
explanations.C: Lower historical reporting accuracy might mean crime was even higher elsewhere, but this attacks data quality rather than explaining the correlation — a 'presupposes what needs to be resolved' trap.
explanations.D: Strategic church attendance as reputation cover is an interesting mechanism but applies to only a small subset of attendees and cannot explain the broader correlation — 'resolves one horn only' at best.
explanations.E: Attendance declining during prosperity confirms a poverty-attendance link but doesn't by itself bridge to crime rates without the second leg of the argument, making this incomplete.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy paradox where a definitional distinction between two superficially similar populations explains divergent moral outcomes.
stimulus: Surveys consistently show that professional ethicists — philosophers who study moral reasoning for a living — are no more likely than non-specialists to donate to charity or to engage in volunteer work. Yet the same ethicists score significantly higher than non-specialists on standardized tests of moral reasoning ability.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Moral reasoning ability, as measured by standardized tests, assesses skill at identifying logical inconsistencies in ethical arguments rather than motivational commitment to acting altruistically.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Professional ethicists earn salaries comparable to those of other academic philosophers, limiting their disposable income for charitable giving.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charitable donation rates vary significantly across different academic disciplines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some professional ethicists specialize in metaethics rather than applied or normative ethics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standardized moral reasoning tests are administered in controlled laboratory settings that may not reflect real-world decision-making.

explanations.correct: The paradox dissolves once 'moral reasoning ability' is recognized as measuring analytical skill at ethical argumentation, not motivation to act morally. Ethicists' high test scores and average donation behavior are entirely consistent because the test measures cognition, not behavioral disposition — a definitional mismatch resolution.
explanations.B: Salary comparability might explain lower donations but doesn't address volunteer work, which requires no financial outlay — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.C: Cross-disciplinary variation is irrelevant to why ethicists in particular score higher but don't give more — an irrelevant-comparison trap.
explanations.D: Metaethics specialization might predict lower applied moral concern, but this applies to only a subset and doesn't resolve the general discrepancy — partial at best.
explanations.E: Lab-setting caveats question the test's validity but don't explain how ethicists can score higher yet behave identically — this merely dismisses one data point rather than reconciling both.

difficultyReason: Economics paradox with a self-selection and composition-effect explanation: aggregate statistics mask shifts in the composition of the measured population.
stimulus: The average salary of workers who leave Portsmith's technology sector for jobs in other industries has risen steadily over the past decade. Yet average salaries within Portsmith's technology sector itself have also risen over the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Workers who leave the technology sector do so primarily for reasons of work-life balance rather than for higher compensation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Over the decade, only the highest-paid technology workers — those who commanded premium salaries in both sectors — chose to leave, so departing workers' rising average salary reflects an increasingly elite outflow rather than rising pay in destination industries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Portsmith's cost of living has risen substantially over the past decade, reducing real wages in both the technology sector and other industries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Workers who remain in the technology sector tend to have more years of experience than those who leave.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Portsmith's government offers tax incentives to technology firms that retain workers for more than five years.

explanations.correct: The rising average salary of departing workers reflects a composition shift: over time, only increasingly well-compensated workers choose to leave, pulling up the departing cohort's average. Meanwhile, in-sector salaries also rise due to standard wage growth. There is no contradiction — the two trends operate independently. Both facts are reconciled by the changing composition of the departing group.
explanations.A: If workers leave for balance rather than pay, this makes it harder to explain why their salaries rose — it doesn't resolve why both averages climb simultaneously and could deepen the paradox.
explanations.C: Rising cost of living affects real wages uniformly and therefore cannot explain the differential pattern between departing and remaining workers — irrelevant to the specific discrepancy.
explanations.D: Experience levels of stayers versus leavers don't directly explain why departing workers' salaries trend upward alongside sector salaries — an incomplete resolution.
explanations.E: Retention incentives might affect who stays but don't address the salary trends of those who depart — 'resolves one horn only.'

difficultyReason: Arts/policy paradox requiring a temporal-scope or funding-mechanism explanation that bridges an apparent contradiction between individual success and institutional decline.
stimulus: Over the past fifteen years, the number of individual visual artists in Grenwick who earn a living solely from the sale of their work has increased by 20 percent. Yet over the same period, the total number of commercial art galleries operating in Grenwick has declined by nearly 40 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cost of renting gallery space in Grenwick has increased substantially over the past fifteen years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Online sales platforms and social media have allowed Grenwick artists to sell directly to collectors worldwide, reducing dependence on physical galleries as intermediaries while simultaneously expanding artists' earning potential.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several large Grenwick galleries that closed were replaced by museum annexes that exhibit but do not sell artwork.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grenwick's municipal government reduced its arts subsidy budget by 15 percent over the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Artists who earn a living solely from artwork sales in Grenwick tend to specialize in portraiture and commissioned pieces.

explanations.correct: Online platforms and social media eliminated the gallery's role as the required sales intermediary. More artists can now earn a living by selling directly to buyers, so artist income rises even as physical gallery numbers fall. The same technological shift explains both horns of the paradox simultaneously.
explanations.A: Rising rental costs explain why galleries closed (one horn) but not why more artists are nonetheless earning a living from their work — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.C: Museum annexes explain some gallery closures but don't address why artist income increased — another 'resolves one horn only' trap.
explanations.D: Reduced subsidies would predict both fewer galleries and fewer self-supporting artists, which deepens the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.E: Specialization in portraiture and commissioned work is irrelevant to the gallery-decline trend — an irrelevant distractor.
